title: In 76,215 human genomes, predicted conserved RNA structures in non-coding DNA show no strong pair-specific selection; primate substitution tests are biased and leave weak selection unresolved
abstract: Human variation gives no evidence that base pairs predicted in conserved RNA structures of human non-coding DNA are under strong selection to stay paired. This matters because such predictions support claims that a large part of the dark genome works as structured RNA (13.6% of the genome, or about 516,000 regions), and they are used to rank non-coding variants. A change at a paired base either keeps the pair (G-C to G-U) or breaks it (G-C to A·C). Test T compares the same mutation (G>A or U>C) at the same base type where it breaks a Watson-Crick pair or keeps a G-U pair, with a within-site control, so mutation rate and sequence constraint cancel; it measures selection on G-U pairs. Test W compares pair-breaking transversions with the wobble-forming transition at the C of G-C and the A of A-U pairs, relative to unpaired bases and to a control; it measures selection on Watson-Crick pairs. For both, 1 means no pair-specific selection. In gnomAD v4.1 (76,215 genomes, non-CpG sites), 127,972 CMfinder structures (CRS) in introns and intergenic DNA give T = 0.996 (95% CI 0.982-1.010) and W = 0.995 (0.986-1.004); RNAfold pairs in random non-conserved DNA give 0.994 and 0.998. Splice-site alleles of loss-of-function-intolerant genes reach an observed/expected ratio of 0.089, so at most 2% of predicted pairs can have splice-like effects, at most 4% effects that halve the ratio, and at most 18-19% effects of 10%. EvoFold gives T = 0.988 and W = 0.967 (0.942-0.992); such 1-4% deficits could be weak selection on a minority of pairs or the choice of slowly mutating columns. Species differences seemed to give strong support (T = 0.31-0.61 in human, chimpanzee and macaque lineages), but the predictors had used these genomes, and random DNA folded on the human sequence still gives T = 0.76 in chimpanzee. We describe three biases and controls: circularity, choice of columns by mutation rate, and polymorphism shared by great apes or orthology differences. In lineages the predictors never saw, T is 0.80-0.99 (0.71-0.79 relative to matched random-DNA controls); these tests see only G-U pairs, so weak selection on a minority of them is not excluded. Limitations: tRNA and microRNA hairpins are too few to act as positive controls; human variation detects only fairly strong selection; the 13.6% set is no longer available.

display.caption: A: T (G-U pairs) and B: W (Watson-Crick pairs) in gnomAD v4.1 (76,215 genomes), non-CpG sites, 95% bootstrap CI over structures. T compares G>A (U>C) where it breaks a G-C (A-U) pair with where it keeps a G-U pair, divided by the same ratio for the other alleles at those bases. W compares pair-breaking transversions with the wobble-forming transition at the C of G-C and the A of A-U pairs, relative to unpaired bases. 1 = no pair-specific selection. Dotted line: value expected if every pair-breaking allele were as harmful as a canonical splice-site loss (observed/expected 0.089).

T for lineage-specific substitutions at predicted pairs. Orange: genomes that the structure predictor used (circular). Blue: genomes it did not use. Green: RNAfold pairs in random non-conserved DNA folded on the human sequence (no function), which show the size of the biases. New base absent: only alleles absent from that column in all other genomes of the CRS alignment. Strict: human also carries the ancestral pair. Panel A reads chimpanzee and gorilla from the CRS alignment; panel B reads all genomes through UCSC pairwise chains.

Largest fraction of predicted pairs in introns and intergenic DNA that is compatible with the 95% interval of T (G-U pairs, solid) or W (Watson-Crick pairs, dashed) in human variation, as a function of the observed/expected ratio of pair-breaking alleles at a selected pair. Blue: CRS; violet: EvoFold. Weak selection (ratio near 1) is not excluded.
